# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more

whys.g1: The group name is plain, and my answer and Eleanor's clearly fit it, but Walter's is mainly about keeping up with lots of people talking, with seeing it first as an afterthought, so it sits a little oddly there and is closer to Ruth's answer about picking up more voices.
whys.g2: There is no real junk on this line, and Tomás's answer, the one that doesn't really address what would make it worth more, was kept out of the group.

founder.order_why: The flow runs well from context to problem to idea to commercial, but 'who has to agree before they can buy' (screen 14) sits apart from 'who decides' (screens 10-11), with cost and price in between, when it belongs right after them.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 overlap: for my wearer-pays product, saying the wearer decides and pays already mostly answers that nobody else has to agree. Screens 15-16 then come back to the same buyer and payer point.
founder.missing: How I actually charge: AirCaps is a one-off hardware purchase from $599 plus a free captions plan or an optional $20/month Pro plan, but I had to force that into a single yearly price of $599 to $839 because the price question has no one-off-plus-subscription option. It also never asked whether HSA/FSA funds can pay, which changes the real out-of-pocket cost for my buyers.

PRIMARY.order_why: It mostly flows from the idea to my habits to price and ordering, but the money questions are labelled 'What you do today' and the follow-up about what would make it worth more interrupts them before the $599 question.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 6 both ask what I would pay up front, and screen 8 covers similar ground as a commitment to buy.
PRIMARY.missing: Whether it works in the places I struggle, like noisy rooms and group talk, how accurate and fast the captions are, what I use today to get by, and whether insurance or a hearing-related benefit could help pay.

screens.why4: The value box and the leave-out chip work, but the hint's "data" and "signature" fit an enterprise sale better than a consumer buying glasses, and a free-returns order is only softly a cost, so the hint does not quite test how much it commits them.
screens.why5: "Order a pair with free returns" is kept word for word, but "Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order... now" stretches my step from people who hit this problem weekly in my segment to nearly everyone, right now.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take: pay a deposit, order a pair with free returns, or book a fitting call? Say what they give up, in up to 25 words.

screens.why1: Right after I named ordering with free returns as the first real step, it makes sense for Keel to show that step back as the last commercial belief it will test.
screens.why2: I can read it at once and 'a pair' is plain to me because I sell glasses, but 'a pair' never says of what, and 'now' leaves me unsure whether it means today or once they have seen the offer.
screens.why3: How many of my customers would order is exactly what I bet on and watch every day through orders and returns, so I can judge this belief from my own work.
screens.why4: The 'probably not or no' bar is clear and I can live with it, but it doesn't match the word 'most', because a result with only 40% yes and the rest unsure would still hold.
screens.why5: My step is kept, but the belief drops the glasses and the $599 price and widens from adults who talk with hearing people every week to all deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, so it claims more than I meant while testing something cheaper-sounding.
screens.instead: Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults who talk with hearing people every week would order a pair of caption glasses at $599 with free returns if they could do it today. (Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.)

screens.why1: Right after I set the first real step as ordering a pair with free returns, and just before the study goes out, it makes sense to decide whether to ask people to act on it.
screens.why2: The choice and the hint's line are clear, but 'pilot' is a slightly odd word for a consumer product you simply order, so I need the hint to see that it means collecting emails.
screens.why3: I know whether I want to follow up with people who say yes, so I can answer this at once from my own plans.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete, distinct and in plain words, and no escape chip is needed for a decision that is mine to make.
screens.why5: My step was 'Order a pair with free returns', but this screen doesn't show it, and the generic 'try this for real, leave your email' is softer than an order, so the commitment has drifted a little.
screens.instead: Ask people who say yes to order a pair with free returns? They get a line at the end: "Would you order a pair with free returns? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Choosing an interviewer makes sense just before the study goes out, but a voice-led choice is abrupt when the people I'm reaching are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, and the screen doesn't acknowledge that.
screens.why2: I can read it on one pass, but 'Keel records her once' and '400 credits' don't say what is recorded or what the credits mean for my budget.
screens.why3: I can listen to both faces and pick one, and I know my customers well enough to judge how a spoken interviewer would land with them.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but my true answer is missing: an interview my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents can read and answer by typing, or at least one with live captions, because a voice they can't follow is the exact problem I'm building for.
screens.why5: The screen doesn't misstate my words, but its generic 'them' and 'hear her' drop the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult I typed in, so it drifts from who I said these people are.
screens.instead: Your respondents are deaf or hard-of-hearing, so how should they take this interview? Options: Read and type | Captions with a voice (Daphne) | Captions with a voice (Saskia)

screens.why1: Once I've decided who asks my questions, it's obvious that I'd choose how people answer before sending the link, and for my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents this choice matters.
screens.why2: I can make the choice on first read, but "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" never says what is being counted, and the stray "recording" tags mean nothing to me.
screens.why3: I know how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents communicate, so I can answer this at once: a voice-led video is the wrong default for many of them, and text works.
screens.why4: My true answer, Text only, is there and the three options are distinct, but the Daphne option is pitched on hearing and audio ("aloud", "Hear it") without saying whether her questions are captioned, which is what I'd need to know before choosing it or letting people choose.
screens.why5: My pick of Text only is kept and nothing misstates my product, but the screen has drifted from the deaf and hard-of-hearing adults I typed in by treating them as people who can listen to a video and be understood when they talk.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? — Text only: they read each question and tap or type | AI interviewer Daphne: on video with every question captioned; they talk, type or tap (she gets nearly all spoken answers right in a quiet room, and over 9 in 10 somewhere loud) | Let them choose when they open the link

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who receives the link.
screens.why2: The question and first option are instantly clear, but 'the Contacts page' and 'Pick a list' assume a part of Keel I have not seen anywhere in this flow, so I would read that option twice.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching out to named people from my own network, such as hard-of-hearing users and testers, or posting in a community, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and an open group link are distinct and cover how I would reach people, and my answer of people I know by name is there without needing an escape chip.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept exactly, and the screen changes nothing about my study or its meaning.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits under the title with "2 of 5 holding" beside it, and the footer says the worst dimension sets the verdict, though "it costs less than you think" could at first read as my glasses being cheap.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but the counts are plain and over 7 people; the bar needs a second look because the cards don't state it, such as the "no more than 1 in 3" I was shown for Commitment.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are my exact lines and Price is recognisably mine, but Existing sacrifice is garbled ("12 conversations of the conversations they are in a month: the conversations they are in"), and the numbering jumps from 4 to 6.
screens.why_b4: Each card says what fell short, such as "they value it below your price", but nothing says what this means for $599 or what to change or test next.
screens.why_b5: The 7 is visible, but nothing says it is a small sample, and "Holding up" on 6 of 7 ordering sits unexplained beside 0 of 7 valuing it at $599, so Commitment looks stronger than it may be.
screens.instead: Not holding up, from only 7 people: 6 would order a pair with free returns, yet none valued it at $599 or $20 a month and only 2 could pay from today's spend, so test a lower price or real orders before trusting the yes.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" is stated outright, and "1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month" sits directly under it and decides it.
screens.why_b2: The seven answers against a mark at 12 are easy to place, but the mangled axis label "conversations of the conversations they are in a month" and the absence of a stated total take a second look.
screens.why_b3: I estimated the existing cost in dollars a year ($200 to $1,500), so "12 conversations of the conversations they are in a month: the conversations they are in" is neither my belief nor my wording, and the "last thing they paid for" tail doesn't fit the question.
screens.why_b4: "They lose less today than you estimated" only restates the result and doesn't say what it means for my $599 glasses, my price or who I should target.
screens.why_b5: The named list and 1 of 7 keep n visible, but "they lose less today" is stated flatly from seven people with no low-n warning, and missed conversations are treated as an existing cost without any spending evidence.
screens.instead: Not holding up, on only 7 people: 1 of 7 missed 12 or more conversations last month (most missed 2 to 8), so this doesn't show the loss is big enough to justify $599; ask what they spend today and talk to more heavy-loss users before relying on it.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside the deciding counts, 0 of 7 at $599 or more once and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, and they agree with the chart.
screens.why_b2: The 7 people and the two counts are plain, but one chart runs the up-front and monthly ladders together, and $599 and $20 each sit on the edge of two bands, so I need a second look to see where my bar falls.
screens.why_b3: The $599 and $20 are my numbers and I recognise the belief, but "then $20 a month" makes my optional Pro plan sound compulsory when captions are free, and the card shows no bar set in my own terms beyond the price.
screens.why_b4: It tells me they value it below my price, and the quotes hint that people want to try a pair first, but it never says whether to change the price, the Pro fee or the trial.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible and nothing is claimed beyond them, but the low n is never called out, and "below your price" hides how close the six in the $250 to $599 band may be to $599.
screens.instead: None of the 7 would pay $599 up front or $20 a month, though 6 put it somewhere from $250 to $599 and several would decide only after trying a pair; only 7 answered, so test a borrow-first trial and a lower entry price before changing the list price, and ask about Pro separately because captions are free.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly beside "2 of 7 from money already there", and that count is plainly the number deciding it.
screens.why_b2: I can see at once that this counts where the $599 would come from across 7 people (2, 5, 0), and what counts for and against me, but no line says how many of the 7 I needed.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay is the name I know and $599 is my price, but the line under it describes what Keel does rather than stating a belief, and "than you thought" never shows what I thought.
screens.why_b4: It tells me fewer could pay from today's spend, but not what that means for me: nobody said they couldn't pay, so the real job is getting them to set aside new money for $599 or lowering the upfront cost.
screens.why_b5: The 7 stays visible and nothing is claimed beyond them, but the small sample is never called out, and a flat "Not holding up" sits over a chart where all 7 could find the money and 0 couldn't pay.
screens.instead: Not holding up, from only 7 people: all 7 could find $599, but only 2 from money they already spend and 5 would have to set new money aside, against a bar of N of 7, so treat this as a new purchase they must budget for and test a lower upfront price or monthly payments.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said it went as you said", so I get the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The counts and the 7 people are plain, but the bar line only repeats my belief, gives no pass mark, and doesn't show which of the four bars count for me, so I have to work out that "No, I decided on my own" is the 6.
screens.why_b3: The name Buyer and payer and the belief line are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: The card says nothing about what this means for the idea, such as selling to the wearer directly and not building for a family or clinic sign-off, so the next step is left for me to infer.
screens.why_b5: The count stays visible and nothing is called strong, but "Holding up" applies an answer about the last thing they paid for to my $599 glasses without saying that earlier purchase may have been far smaller, or that 7 people is few.
screens.instead: Holding up: 6 of 7 decided their last purchase for this alone, and 1 needed someone else's agreement, so keep selling to the wearer, but with only 7 people and a past purchase that may have cost far less than $599, this doesn't yet show they'd decide alone at that price.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes", so I get both the verdict and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The four bars and the count of 7 are plain, but the bar line only repeats "order a pair with free returns" and never gives my threshold of no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no, so I have to work out where the bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The title is Commitment and the belief line is word for word the one I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what this result means for the idea or what I should do next, least of all how to square it with the Price card's 0 of 7 at $599.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and the count is honest, but "Holding up" rests on a question that names no price, with no caution about the small sample or that 0 of 7 valued it at $599, so it overstates how real these orders are.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only as a no-price answer: 6 of 7 would order with free returns (bar: no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no), yet 0 of 7 valued it at $599, so re-ask with $599 in the question before you count these as orders; and label each person "Yes, I'd order a pair", not "Yes, I'd start one".

screens.why_b1: Every line has its status word, and Buyer and payer and Commitment show 6 of 7, but Price, the line that failed, shows no deciding number here, only group counts of 3 and 3 and the answer ranges under each quote.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are the ones I checked and the quotes are in my customers' language, but my belief lines are missing, so I have to remember that Commitment meant ordering a pair with free returns and Buyer and payer meant the wearer decides alone.
screens.why_b4: The 'Try a pair first to see it works' group points me toward demos or loaner pairs, but the screen never says what the failed Price line means for my $599 and $20 a month, so I have to draw the conclusion myself.
screens.why_b5: Counts stay small and visible, but Walter's family-lunch quote sits under WHO HAD TO AGREE as the reason for his 'someone else had to agree' answer when it says nothing about anyone agreeing, and the Price line never states its 7 people.
screens.why_b6: I learned things I did not type: people want to test a pair in their own hard situation before ordering even though I offer free returns, stage lights and audience questions are specific tests of whether it works, and a single-sided user's end-seat workaround is a real competitor to my glasses.
screens.instead: Price did not hold: 0 of 7 would pay $599 up front, and most answers fell at $250 to $599 once and under $20 a month; 3 of 7 want to try a pair in their own hard setting first (a noisy walk, a matinee, a big family lunch), so test a loaner or demo pair before you change the price.

screens.why1: As the first question, it makes sense to check straight away whether I regularly talk with hearing people, because that is who the study seems to be for.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I would say it myself, and I can answer the question the first time I read it.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I talk with hearing people each week, because it is part of my ordinary life.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct and cover the whole answer for a weekly habit, and a screening question like this does not need an escape option.
screens.why5: It asks only about my weekly conversations and does not reveal any product, company plan or label for people like me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a simple yes-or-no answer, so it is easy to take in the first time, though I would want the words on screen too because I may not catch them by ear.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; No

screens.why1: After being asked whether I talk with hearing people every week, showing me an idea for following those conversations is an obvious next step, and the kicker tells me that is what it is.
screens.why2: Glasses, live captions and eye contact are everyday words for me as a deaf person, and I would get it on one read or from the screen while it is spoken.
screens.why3: I live with captions and with losing eye contact when I look down at a phone or interpreter, so I can picture this in my own conversations.
screens.why4: The card shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is a deliberate idea card that names the product and says what it does and what its builders believe, and nothing reaches me outside that frame; "the wearer" is a little stiff but not a leak.
screens.why6: The short sentences say well and hold in one hearing, but the last one, "would mean the wearer reads the words while keeping eye contact", is a bit of a mouthful and "the wearer" sounds odd after being spoken to as "you".
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps. You wear lightweight glasses while the people nearby talk. An app on the glasses shows live captions of what they are saying, inside the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, under 'What you do today', it makes sense to ask how much I lose to this problem now.
screens.why2: 'Miss' is the unclear word, because I rarely miss a whole conversation but often lose parts of one or give up halfway, so I'd have to stop and work out what counts.
screens.why3: This happens to me all the time and nobody keeps count, so a figure for a whole month would be a guess, though a week would be easier to estimate.
screens.why4: The number box, 'None' and 'I can't recall' all fit, but 'I'd rather not say' is an odd extra on a harmless count and is a second way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'conversations did you miss' has drifted from conversations that were too fast or too noisy to follow, and 'last month' has replaced the last 7 days.
screens.why6: It is short, a single question with one escape, and easy to answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, about how many conversations with hearing people were too fast or too noisy to follow? [number box; chips: None; I can't recall]

screens.why1: Asking what it's worth makes sense after the idea card, but it comes abruptly after counting missed conversations and sits under a 'What you do today' heading, when this isn't something I do today.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are plain, and I understand the question on first reading, though the 'once' after each price is a little stiff.
screens.why3: I know what missing conversations costs me and what I'd spend on my hearing needs, but I'd partly be guessing at a price for glasses I've only read about on a card and never worn.
screens.why4: The ranges cover everything and read naturally, but they share edges: $599 and $1,000 each fall in two options, as do $20 and $50 on the monthly list.
screens.why5: The name AirCaps comes from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: Each question is short, but six dollar-range options are too many to hold after one hearing, 'Under $250 once' sounds awkward, 'Or say I can't say' is clumsy, and the monthly question's spoken form leaves out the escape.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250; $250 to $598; $599 to $999; $1,000 to $2,500; or over $2,500. Or say I can't say. Then: And after that, what would it be worth each month? Under $10; $10 to $19; $20 to $49; $50 to $100; or over $100. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: I just gave a price, so asking what would make it worth more is an obvious follow-up to that answer.
screens.why2: Short everyday words that I can answer on first reading, and the price echoes back the range I picked.
screens.why3: I can say what I would need from captions in a noisy room, but I have only read a card about AirCaps and never used it, so part of my answer is a guess.
screens.why4: There are no options, only a box to type in.
screens.why5: The product name and price are the ones already shown to me on the idea card and the last question, so nothing new leaks and the question stays on what it is worth.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but "$250 to $599 once" is a little clumsy to hear, and the word "once" comes across oddly at the end of the sentence.
screens.instead: You said AirCaps would be worth $250 to $599 up front. What would make it worth more to you?

screens.why1: I just put AirCaps at up to $599, so asking whether I could actually pay that is the obvious next question, even if the 'What you do today' label doesn't quite match.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but I'd have to read 'money you already spend' twice because it doesn't say spend on what, and I don't have a budget for captions.
screens.why3: I know what I can afford and what I already spend on my hearing needs, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and my answer is there, but 'on this' is vague because I don't spend on AirCaps yet, and insurance or vocational rehab paying isn't covered, though 'I can't say' fits well enough.
screens.why5: It stays with the price I just gave and the idea I was shown, and no company plans or odd labels for people reach me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with three short options I can hold after one hearing, and '$599' says fine as a spoken price.
screens.instead: Could you pay about $599 once for AirCaps, or not? From what I already spend on my hearing needs; From other money I'd set aside; or I couldn't pay it. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: After the question about paying $599 it makes sense to ask who has a say, but for my own hearing gear it comes across as an abrupt, business-style question.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but I have to stop and work out whether "something like this" means hearing aids, a captioning app or captioning glasses.
screens.why3: I can answer if I count my hearing aids or a captioning app, but I've never bought anything quite like this, so I'd be guessing at what counts.
screens.why4: "Someone else" and "several people" overlap, "someone else decided for me" doesn't really answer whether anyone had to agree, and there's no clear option for insurance or a program having to approve it.
screens.why5: The question stays on who has to agree to a purchase, and no product name or company language reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short and has only four options, but the order flips between yes and no, so the two yes options are hard to hold and compare on one hearing.
screens.instead: The last time you bought hearing or captioning gear for yourself, did anyone else have to agree? No, I decided alone; Yes, one other person; Yes, several people; Yes, insurance or a program. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: After the questions about what I'd pay and who has to agree, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually order, though the 'What you do today' label doesn't fit a question about what I would do.
screens.why2: 'Order a pair with free returns' is plain, and I know from the idea card that a pair means the AirCaps glasses.
screens.why3: I can answer this from my own life, because I know whether I'd risk an order on glasses that might help me follow conversations if I could send them back.
screens.why4: There's a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes' or unsure option, so the choices lean towards no, and I'd have to choose between a firm yes and a no even if I'd want to know more first.
screens.why5: It stays with the idea I was shown, using the name from the card and an ordinary offer, with no company language or labels for people like me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three options that are easy to hold, though the first option repeats 'free returns' from the question.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order a pair; Probably would, but not sure yet; Probably not; or No.
